analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run public health insurance plan to compete with private plans on the ACA exchanges.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee it was sent to, dying without a markup or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The CHOICE Act would have directed the federal government to offer its own health insurance plan — silver and gold plans, with all the standard benefits and consumer protections — on the ACA marketplaces, alongside private insurers. The plan would set premiums by geography, negotiate payment rates with doctors and hospitals (falling back to Medicare rates if talks failed), and automatically include any provider already in Medicare or Medicaid unless that provider opted out. It was referred to the Senate Health Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying coverage on the ACA exchanges — including the uninsured and those priced out of private plans — would gain a government-run alternative with standard benefits, and competition from a public plan could pressure private insurers' premiums. Providers in Medicare and Medicaid would gain a new stream of enrollees by default unless they opted out.

how_it_helps.text: Requires CMS to offer a public plan through the exchanges that meets all federal plan requirements, with silver and gold plans (bronze optional), essential benefits, and cost-sharing limits [S2].
The plan must comply with ACA consumer protections and cost-sharing rules, and state laws banning it would be preempted [S3].

Premiums would be geographically adjusted and could only vary as ACA rules allow, and the plan would be self-financing through premiums, with startup funding repaid to the Treasury over 10 years [S3].
Providers in Medicare or Medicaid would automatically participate unless they opt out, broadening the network available to enrollees [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would lose market share to a public competitor; hospitals and drug makers would face payment rates negotiated by the government, with Medicare rates as the fallback, which typically pay less than private rates. Taxpayers would front startup reserves for the plan, though the bill requires those funds to be repaid over 10 years.

drawbacks.text: The plan must fully finance its own benefit and administrative costs from premiums, so its affordability depends entirely on the government succeeding in negotiating lower provider rates — providers could decline to negotiate, though Medicare rates would then apply [S3].

If negotiations fail, providers would be paid original Medicare fee-for-service rates, which are generally lower than private insurance rates — a real cost cut for hospitals and physicians that could strain providers, particularly those already operating on thin margins [S3].
Taxpayers would be on the hook for startup funding covering 90 days of claims reserves until it is repaid over a 10-year amortization [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives exchange shoppers a guaranteed public alternative with full ACA protections, at little ongoing cost to taxpayers since premiums must cover the plan's costs. The main trade-off is that its savings come from paying providers less — close to Medicare rates if negotiations stall — and insurers and hospital groups would argue a government plan competes on uneven footing. The design is relatively conventional for a public option; the bigger question is political, and Congress never tested it.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Health Committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, so the bill sat there until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on April 4, 2019, joined by original cosponsors including Sherrod Brown, Tammy Baldwin, Dick Durbin, Robert Menendez, and Kamala Harris [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day — the only action it ever received [S5].
Eight Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].
The committee took no further action, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 116th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and hospital systems, which kept the individual market to themselves with no government-run competitor entering it. Exchange shoppers who might have switched to a cheaper public plan are in the same position as before.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a public health insurance option on the ACA exchanges.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee (Republican-led)
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander (R-TN)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill received no action after referral and died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican backed the bill, and the Republican-chaired committee gave it no action.

industries.note: A government-run plan competing on the same exchanges would draw enrollees from private insurers and pressure their premiums. Insurers' revenue depends on exchange plans costing more than a comparable public option would.

Providers would gain a new pool of covered patients through automatic participation, but payment rates would be government-negotiated with Medicare rates as the fallback — generally below private rates. Providers could opt out entirely.
The government would negotiate drug payment rates, falling back to Medicare rates if talks fail, reducing what the plan pays for prescriptions below typical private-market prices.
